title: JVM Runtime
description: OpenMRS backend JVM health, sourced from the OpenTelemetry Java agent over OTLP. Metric and attribute names follow OpenTelemetry semantic conventions, so this dashboard works against any OTLP-compatible backend, not just this stack's Alloy + Prometheus pair.

panels.title: Heap Used %
panels.description: Live heap in use as a percentage of the maximum heap the JVM is allowed to grow to (-Xmx). This is the single most useful top-line number on this dashboard: it is self-scaling, so it stays meaningful without being retuned per deployment. Amber above 75%, red above 90%. If it sits red and 'Heap After Last GC' does not fall back down, the JVM cannot reclaim the space — raise -Xmx or hunt for a leak.

targets.expr: 100 * sum(jvm_memory_used_bytes{job="$job", instance="$instance", jvm_memory_type="heap"}) / max(jvm_memory_limit_bytes{job="$job", instance="$instance", jvm_memory_type="heap"})

panels.title: Heap Used
panels.description: Live heap memory in use right now, summed across all heap pools (G1 Eden, Survivor and Old Gen). Read this alongside 'Heap Used %' — the absolute figure tells you how much memory the container actually needs, which is what you size -Xmx and the container memory limit against.

panels.title: Live Threads
panels.description: Total live JVM threads, summed across every thread state. A healthy app plateaus after warm-up. A count that keeps climbing and never falls back points to a thread leak (often an unbounded or misconfigured thread pool) that will eventually exhaust OS limits — check 'Threads by State' to see which state is growing, then capture a thread dump.

panels.title: Classes Loaded
panels.description: Classes currently loaded by the JVM. Should rise during startup and module loading, then flatten. Continuous growth at steady state signals a classloader leak (common after repeated hot redeploys) and heads toward Metaspace exhaustion — cross-check the Metaspace series in 'Memory Pools Used', then plan a restart and investigate.

panels.title: Heap vs Non-Heap Used
panels.description: JVM memory in use split by area. Heap holds application objects and is garbage-collected; non-heap holds class metadata, the code cache and compressed class space. The dashed red line is the maximum heap (-Xmx). If heap used repeatedly climbs to it and GC only briefly frees space, the app is memory-starved: raise -Xmx or fix a leak. A healthy heap shows a sawtooth — grows, then drops sharply at each GC.

panels.title: Memory Pools Used
panels.description: Used bytes per JVM memory pool, stacked. 'G1 Eden Space' and 'G1 Survivor Space' hold short-lived young objects and are expected to churn constantly. Watch 'G1 Old Gen': if it stays high immediately after a GC and trends upward, long-lived objects are accumulating — a likely leak. Steadily growing 'Metaspace' means a classloader leak instead.

panels.title: GC Time Rate
panels.description: Fraction of wall-clock time spent in garbage collection, per collector (seconds of GC per second; 0.05 = 5%). Brief spikes are normal. Sustained values above roughly 5–10% mean the app is spending real time paused in GC, which surfaces as request latency — a signal to increase heap, fix a leak, or tune the collector. Note that 'G1 Concurrent GC' runs alongside the application and is far less costly than a young or full pause.

panels.title: GC Collections Rate
panels.description: Garbage-collection cycles per second, per collector. Frequent young-generation collections ('G1 Young Generation') are normal and cheap. A rising rate of concurrent or full collections indicates the heap is filling faster than it can be reclaimed — a strong sign of memory pressure or a leak. Read together with 'GC Time Rate': many cheap collections are fine, few expensive ones are not.

panels.title: Threads by State
panels.description: Live threads broken down by JVM thread state, stacked. A large and stable 'timed_waiting' or 'waiting' population is normal — that is idle pool workers parked between jobs. Growth in 'runnable' tracks real load. A total that climbs without ever levelling off is a thread leak; a sudden jump in 'blocked' means threads are contending on a lock and requests will be queueing behind it.

panels.title: JVM CPU Utilization
panels.description: Recent CPU utilisation of the JVM process as reported by the JVM itself, as a fraction of all CPUs available to the container (100% means every core is saturated, not one core). Sustained values near the ceiling mean the JVM is CPU-bound — check for busy loops, GC thrash (cross-reference 'GC Time Rate'), or the need to scale out. Unlike a rate over a CPU-time counter, this needs no window and reacts immediately.

panels.title: Heap After Last GC
panels.description: Bytes still occupied in each heap pool immediately after the most recent garbage collection — the clearest leak signal on this dashboard. Unlike 'Memory Pools Used', this strips out short-lived garbage, so it shows only what the collector could not reclaim. 'G1 Eden Space' should sit at or near zero. A 'G1 Old Gen' line that trends steadily upward over hours, never returning to its earlier baseline, means live objects are accumulating and the JVM will eventually hit OutOfMemoryError — take a heap dump before restarting.
